ABSTRACT
The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) in material design and engineering has led to significant improvements in predictive
modeling of material properties. However, the lack of interpretability in machine learning (ML)‐based material informatics presents
a major barrier to its practical adoption. This study proposes a novel quantitative computational framework that integrates ML
models with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques to enhance both predictive accuracy and interpretability in material
property prediction. The framework systematically incorporates a structured pipeline, including data processing, feature selection,
model training, performance evaluation, explainability analysis, and real‐world deployment. It is validated through a representative
case study on the prediction of high‐performance concrete (HPC) compressive strength, utilizing a comparative analysis of ML
models such as Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). The results
demonstrate that XGBoost achieves the highest predictive performance (R = 0.918

and LIME (Local Interpretable Model‐Agnostic Explanations) provide detailed insights into feature importance and material
interactions. Additionally, the deployment of the trained model as a cloud‐based Flask‐Gunicorn API enables real‐time inference,
ensuring its scalability and accessibility for industrial and research applications. The proposed framework addresses key limitations
of existing ML approaches by integrating advanced explainability techniques, systematically handling nonlinear feature interac-
tions, and providing a scalable deployment strategy. This study contributes to the development of interpretable and deployable
AI‐driven material informatics, bridging the gap between data‐driven predictions and fundamental material science principles.

Introduction
Material design and engineering applications play a pivotal role
in advancing modern technology by developing materials with
tailored properties for diverse industries, including construc-
tion, aerospace, automotive, and biomedical engineering [1–6].
Traditionally, material development has relied on experimental
trial‐and‐error approaches, empirical models, and domain
expertise to optimize performance [7–10]. Conventional meth-
odologies include laboratory‐based experimentation, finite ele-
ment simulations, thermodynamic modeling, and physics‐based
analytical methods [11–14]. While these approaches have been
instrumental in shaping material science, they suffer from
high costs, time‐intensive processes, and inherent limitations
in capturing complex structure–property relationships [15].

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and

discovery, optimizing process parameters, and enhancing per-

adopting AI‐driven approaches in material design is their lack

art ML models, such as ensemble methods (e.g., Random Forest
[RF], eXtreme Gradient Boosting [XGBoost]), deep neural net-
works (DNNs), and support vector regression (SVR), function as
black‐box systems, making it difficult to extract meaningful
insights into the underlying physicochemical principles gov-
erning material behavior [25, 26]. This highlights the urgent
demand for advanced, interpretable, and scientifically grounded
AI techniques capable of delivering reliable insights for material
design and engineering applications [27, 28].
Explainable AI (XAI) has emerged as a transformative paradigm
aimed at enhancing model interpretability while maintaining
predictive accuracy. Various XAI techniques, including SHapley

Dangayach et al. [32] utilized SHAP and LIME to improve

research that prioritizes predictive accuracy at the expense of
interpretability, this framework systematically incorporates

ensuring AI‐driven predictions align with the underlying
physical and chemical principles of material behavior rather
than functioning as a black‐box model [48]. The framework

To demonstrate its effectiveness, the proposed framework is
applied to a representative case study: the prediction of high‐

strength is influenced by complex, multivariable interactions
between material composition, curing conditions, and chemical
reactions, making it an ideal test case for interpretable
AI‐driven modeling [49]. Despite the availability of extensive
experimental datasets, existing approaches lack a unified and
explainable predictive framework that consolidates these data-
sets into a generalizable and scientifically interpretable model
[50]. In this study, SHAP‐based feature importance, SHAP
interaction values, and LIME instance‐level explanations are
leveraged to systematically identify and quantify key material
contributions, ensuring transparency and trustworthiness in
AI‐driven predictions.

interpretability, and computational efficiency. To ensure real‐
world usability, the trained models are deployed in a cloud‐based
API using Flask and Gunicorn, providing scalable, real‐time
access to AI‐driven material property predictions [53]. By sys-
tematically integrating XAI methodologies into the material
engineering workflow, this study bridges the gap between

Framework Architecture and Workflow
The integration of ML and XAI has the potential to revolutionize
material design and engineering applications by providing accu-
rate predictions and interpretable insights into material behavior.
This section presents a structured, modular computational
framework that combines advanced ML techniques with XAI
methodologies to facilitate the reliable and interpretable predic-
tion of material properties.
The proposed framework follows a structured pipeline encom-
passing data preparation, feature selection, model training,
performance evaluation, explainability analysis, and deploy-
ment. This section details each stage, outlining its objectives,
methodologies, and integration within the overall workflow. A
schematic representation of the proposed workflow is provided
in Figure 1, illustrating the sequential execution and interaction
between different components.

Machine Learning Modeling, and Deployment. The data
processing layer handles data collection, preprocessing, and
transformation to ensure high‐quality inputs for model training
[54]. The ML modeling layer incorporates multiple predictive
algorithms, including interpretable models such as linear
regression and decision trees, alongside complex models like
XGBoost and DNNs. Explainability techniques such as SHAP
and LIME are integrated at this stage to ensure model trans-
parency. Finally, the deployment layer provides a cloud‐based
infrastructure for real‐time inference, utilizing Flask‐based
APIs and Gunicorn for scalable processing. This architecture
ensures an end‐to‐end workflow that is adaptable, interpretable,
and deployable for real‐world material design applications [55].

Workflow Components
2.2.1
|
Data Processing Layer
Data Preparation ensures the reliability and consistency of
input variables by collecting and aggregating experimental and
literature‐based datasets. Statistical imputation was applied to
handle missing values, and outliers were detected and removed
to improve model robustness. Numerical variables are nor-
malized, and categorical features (if applicable) are encoded
using standard transformations to standardize feature distri-
butions. Finally, the data set is split into training and testing
subsets to prevent data leakage and facilitate unbiased model
evaluation. Feature Selection and Dimensionality Reduction play
a crucial role in improving model interpretability and compu-
tational efficiency. Correlation analysis (Pearson, Spearman,
Kendall) identifies collinear variables, while Sobol sensitivity
analysis quantifies the importance of material components in
predicting target properties. PCA is applied to reduce data
dimensionality while preserving variance, allowing for effective
model training without losing critical information.
2.2.2
|
ML Layer
Model training is conducted using both interpretable and
complex ML models to balance accuracy and explainability.
While linear regression and decision trees provide transparent
mathematical formulations, more advanced models such as RF,
XGBoost, SVR, and DNNs capture intricate nonlinear relation-
ships among material properties. Hyperparameter tuning, lever-
aging grid search and cross‐validation, is performed to optimize
model parameters and enhance generalization. Performance eva-
luation employs multiple metrics, including mean absolute error
(MAE) for assessing average predictive error, root mean squared
error (RMSE) for penalizing larger deviations, and the coefficient
of determination (R2) to measure model explanatory power. Ex-
plainability analysis integrates SHAP and LIME to provide both
global and local interpretability, ensuring that the AI‐driven
predictions align with physical and chemical principles. SHAP
quantifies feature importance and interaction effects, while LIME
generates instance‐specific explanations, reinforcing model trust-
worthiness. Finally, Results Comparison and Decision Support
systematically evaluates different models based on predictive
accuracy, feature influence, and computational complexity. This
process ensures that the selected model produces scientifically
valid and actionable insights for material design applications.

|
Deployment Layer
Deployment and optimization enable real‐time implementation
of the trained model for practical engineering use. A Flask‐
based REST API provides remote access to AI‐driven material
property

ing automated retraining to maintain accuracy and reliability.
This deployment strategy ensures that the proposed framework
is scalable, accessible, and adaptable to evolving material sci-
ence challenges.

Data Preparation
Data preparation ensured data set quality, consistency, and
reliability for predictive modeling. The data set, compiled from
multiple experimental studies, was preprocessed to resolve
inconsistencies across sources. Key steps included handling
missing values, removing outliers, and standardizing data types.
Feature engineering techniques—normalization, standardiza-
tion, scaling, and interaction terms—were applied to improve
model performance.
To ensure robust evaluation and prevent overfitting, stratified
sampling allocated 75% of the data for training and 25% for testing.
Additionally, 10‐fold cross‐validation was employed to assess
model generalizability and guide hyperparameter optimization.

HPC strength is influenced by multiple factors, including material
composition, mixing proportions, and preparation techniques.
While extensive experimental data exist, there is no unified model
consolidating these data sets into a predictive framework. Addi-
tionally, many data sets lack complete descriptions of mix prop-
erties, making direct strength prediction a challenging task.
In this study, the compressive strength of HPC is modeled as a
function of the following eight input features:

2. Fly ash (kg/m3): supplementary cementitious material
(SCM) affecting long‐term strength.

5. Superplasticizer (kg/m3): improves fluidity and reduces
water content.
6. Coarse aggregate (kg/m3): large particles contributing to
the concrete matrix.
7. Fine aggregate (kg/m3): fills voids and enhances strength.
8. Age of testing (days): curing period affecting strength

LIME analysis further explains feature importance in predicting
concrete compressive strength. As shown in Figure 16, age and
cement content are the most influential factors, with age having
the highest impact due to continued hydration. Water is crucial

reducing water demand, though excessive dosages can delay
setting. Blast furnace slag contributes to strength but varies
across mixtures, while fly ash shows the lowest importance due
to its delayed pozzolanic reaction, making its effects less
prominent in datasets with shorter curing periods.

This study presents a quantitative computational framework
that integrates ML and XAI techniques to enhance the
accuracy, interpretability, and scalability of AI‐driven material
design. The proposed framework systematically addresses
the challenges associated with existing ML‐based material
property prediction models, particularly their lack of inter-
pretability, inadequate handling of nonlinear feature interac-

framework incorporates a structured pipeline consisting of data
processing, feature selection, model training, performance
evaluation, explainability analysis, and deployment, ensuring a
comprehensive and scientifically grounded approach to mate-
rial informatics.

study on the prediction of HPC compressive strength, dem-

Limitations and Future Work
While the proposed framework provides significant advance-
ments in AI‐driven material design, several limitations exist.
First, the framework primarily relies on supervised ML models,
which require high‐quality labeled data. Future work explores
semi‐supervised and unsupervised learning techniques to lever-
age unlabeled material datasets. Second, while SHAP and LIME
offer robust interpretability, additional XAI techniques such as
counterfactual explanations and attention mechanisms in deep
learning could further enhance the interpretability of complex
models. Third, this study focuses on a single case study
(HPC compressive strength prediction); expanding the frame-
work to other material systems such as metal alloys, polymers,
and composite materials validates its generalizability. Finally,

Abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) in material design and engineering has led to significant improvements in predictive modeling of material properties. However, the lack of interpretability in machine learning (ML)‐based material informatics presents a major barrier to its practical adoption. This study proposes a novel quantitative computational framework that integrates ML models with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques to enhance both predictive accuracy and interpretability in material property prediction. The framework systematically incorporates a structured pipeline, including data processing, feature selection, model training, performance evaluation, explainability analysis, and real‐world deployment. It is validated through a representative case study on the prediction of high‐performance concrete (HPC) compressive strength, utilizing a comparative analysis of ML models such as Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). The results demonstrate that XGBoost achieves the highest predictive performance (R = 0.918 2 ), while SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model‐Agnostic Explanations) provide detailed insights into feature importance and material interactions. Additionally, the deployment of the trained model as a cloud‐based Flask‐Gunicorn API enables real‐time inference, ensuring its scalability and accessibility for industrial and research applications. The proposed framework addresses key limitations of existing ML approaches by integrating advanced explainability techniques, systematically handling nonlinear feature interac- tions, and providing a scalable deployment strategy. This study contributes to the development of interpretable and deployable AI‐driven material informatics, bridging the gap between data‐driven predictions and fundamental material science principles.
